subject: Biology
title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
summary: Anatomy is the study of the internal structure of plants. The rationalised chapter covers the three tissue systems (epidermal, ground and vascular) and then the transverse sections of the dicot root, monocot root, dicot stem, monocot stem, dorsiventral leaf and isobilateral leaf. It is a diagram-driven chapter: almost every question is really asking you to draw a section, label it in NCERT words and compare monocot with dicot.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Anatomy of Flowering Plants sits in Unit II, Structural Organisation in Plants and Animals, which carries 11 marks shared with Morphology of Flowering Plants and Structural Organisation in Animals. In a typical school final this chapter contributes about 4 to 6 marks: a 1-mark MCQ or Assertion–Reason, a 2-mark or 3-mark comparison (dicot versus monocot root, stem or leaf) and, in many papers, a 5-mark question asking for a labelled transverse section. In NEET it is a steady source of one or two questions, usually lifted straight from the NCERT descriptions of the sections and the vascular bundle types.

question_types.note: Identify the layer from a feature (casparian strips, starch sheath, bulliform cells, lateral-root origin), the vascular bundle type of a given organ (radial, conjoint open, conjoint closed), exarch versus endarch protoxylem, polyarch roots, and which organ lacks phloem parenchyma or has water-containing cavities.

Guard-cell wall thickness and stomatal movement; absence of cuticle in roots; why monocot stems and roots show no secondary growth; why dicot stem vascular bundles are called open; why the endodermis of a dicot stem is called a starch sheath.

Define stomatal apparatus, bulliform cells, casparian strips, conjunctive tissue, stele; distinguish radial from conjoint bundles; state two differences between dicot and monocot root; name the origin of root hairs and lateral roots.

Three differences between a dicot and a monocot stem (or root, or leaf) in a table; describe the epidermal tissue system; describe the vascular bundle of a monocot stem; identify an organ from a list of anatomical features and justify.

Draw and describe the T.S. of a dicot root or dicot stem or the V.S. of a dorsiventral leaf; compare dicot and monocot stem with labelled diagrams; describe the three tissue systems with the tissues under each.

A passage describing a section seen under the microscope or a leaf under water stress, followed by identify-and-justify sub-questions on vascular bundle arrangement, bundle sheath, bulliform cells or the endodermis.

sections.heading: Introduction: what plant anatomy is, and the tissues you need to recognise
sections.body:
You can see the outside of a plant easily. To see the inside you cut a thin section and put it under a microscope. The study of the internal structure of plants is called anatomy. Plants are built from cells; cells are organised into tissues; tissues are organised into organs. Different organs (root, stem, leaf) differ in their internal structure, and within angiosperms the monocots and dicots are also anatomically different. Internal structure also shows adaptations to different environments, which is why a grass leaf looks different from a mango leaf when sectioned.

The rationalised NCERT chapter opens directly with the tissue systems, and the older detailed treatment of meristems, simple and complex tissues and secondary growth has been removed from the CBSE syllabus. But the chapter still uses those names on every page, so you need the following as background. A tissue is a group of cells having a common origin and usually performing a common function. On the basis of the ability to divide there are two kinds: meristematic tissue (cells that keep dividing: apical meristems at root and shoot tips give primary growth; intercalary meristems between mature tissues in grasses regenerate parts eaten by cattle; lateral meristems such as vascular cambium and cork cambium give increase in girth) and permanent tissue (cells that have lost the ability to divide and have taken a fixed shape and function).

Permanent tissues are simple when made of one cell type: parenchyma (thin cellulose walls, living, storage, photosynthesis, packing), collenchyma (living, walls thickened at the corners with cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin, gives mechanical support to growing parts such as the young stem and petiole) and sclerenchyma (dead at maturity, thick lignified walls, as fibres and sclereids, gives strength). They are complex when several cell types work together: xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma; conducts water and minerals upward and gives mechanical strength) and phloem (sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres; conducts food from leaves to the rest of the plant). Two xylem words appear again and again: the first-formed xylem is protoxylem and the later-formed is metaxylem. When protoxylem lies towards the centre and metaxylem towards the periphery, as in stems, the arrangement is endarch; when protoxylem lies towards the periphery and metaxylem towards the centre, as in roots, it is exarch. These terms are still examined in NEET and are used freely in the sections that follow.

formulas.expr: Anatomy = study of internal structure; cells → tissues → organs
where: group of cells with a common origin, usually a common function

formulas.expr: Endarch: protoxylem towards centre (stems). Exarch: protoxylem towards periphery (roots)

sections.tip: Even though meristems and secondary growth are out of the CBSE syllabus, never write 'cambium is absent in dicot stems'. The rationalised chapter still says dicot stem bundles are open because cambium is present.

sections.heading: 6.1 The Tissue System
sections.body:
Tissues can be classified by the kinds of cells they contain, which is what the background above did. NCERT now asks a different question: how do tissues vary depending on their location in the plant body? Their structure and function depend on where they sit. On the basis of structure and location, there are three tissue systems: the epidermal tissue system, the ground or fundamental tissue system and the vascular or conducting tissue system.

Think of any organ in transverse section as three concentric zones. The outermost skin is the epidermal system. Everything inside the skin that is not a vascular bundle is the ground system: cortex, endodermis, pericycle, pith and medullary rays in stems and roots, and the mesophyll in leaves. The strands of xylem and phloem, wherever they are placed, are the vascular system. Every T.S. you draw in this chapter is just these three systems arranged in the pattern characteristic of that organ, so if you learn the three systems well the six sections in 6.2 become a matter of arrangement rather than new material.

The examiner's standard 3-mark or 5-mark question here is the old NCERT exercise: name the three basic tissue systems and give the tissue names under each. Answer it as a table. Epidermal: epidermis (epidermal cells), stomata (guard cells and subsidiary cells), epidermal appendages (root hairs, trichomes), cuticle. Ground: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, forming cortex, hypodermis, endodermis, pericycle, pith, medullary rays, mesophyll. Vascular: xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma) and phloem (sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres) arranged in vascular bundles, with cambium in open bundles.

formulas.expr: Three tissue systems (by structure and location): epidermal, ground (fundamental), vascular (conducting)
where: outer covering: epidermis, stomata, hairs, cuticle
all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles

sections.tip: NCERT classifies the systems 'on the basis of their structure and location'. Write that phrase; it is the definition the marking scheme looks for.

sections.heading: 6.1.1 Epidermal Tissue System
sections.body:
The epidermal tissue system forms the outermost covering of the whole plant body. It comprises the epidermal cells, the stomata and the epidermal appendages (trichomes and hairs).

The epidermis is the outermost layer of the primary plant body and is usually single-layered. Its cells are parenchymatous, with a small amount of cytoplasm lining the cell wall and a large vacuole. The outside of the epidermis is often covered with a waxy, thick layer called the cuticle, which prevents loss of water. The cuticle is absent in roots, which makes sense because the root epidermis has to absorb water rather than hold it in.

Stomata are structures present in the epidermis of leaves. They regulate the processes of transpiration and gaseous exchange. Each stoma is composed of two bean-shaped cells called guard cells which enclose the stomatal pore. In grasses the guard cells are dumb-bell shaped. The outer walls of the guard cells (away from the stomatal pore) are thin and the inner walls (towards the stomatal pore) are highly thickened. This unequal thickening is what lets the guard cells bend outward when turgid and open the pore, and straighten when flaccid and close it. Guard cells possess chloroplasts and regulate the opening and closing of stomata. Sometimes a few epidermal cells in the vicinity of the guard cells become specialised in their shape and size and are known as subsidiary cells. The stomatal aperture, the guard cells and the surrounding subsidiary cells together are called the stomatal apparatus. That definition is a favourite 1-mark and 2-mark question.

The cells of the epidermis bear a number of hairs. Root hairs are unicellular elongations of the epidermal cells and help absorb water and minerals from the soil. On the stem the epidermal hairs are called trichomes. Trichomes in the shoot system are usually multicellular; they may be branched or unbranched, soft or stiff, and may even be secretory. Trichomes help in preventing water loss due to transpiration. So the contrast the examiner wants is: root hair = unicellular, absorption; trichome = multicellular, on the stem, reduces water loss.

formulas.expr: Stomatal apparatus = stomatal aperture + two guard cells + subsidiary cells
where: bean-shaped (dicots), dumb-bell shaped (grasses); outer wall thin, inner wall thick; have chloroplasts
epidermal cells near guard cells, specialised in shape and size

formulas.expr: Root hair: unicellular, absorbs water and minerals. Trichome: multicellular, on stem, prevents water loss, may be secretory

sections.tip: Students write 'inner wall thin, outer wall thick'. It is the reverse: the wall towards the pore is thick. Draw the thick wall as a heavier line next to the pore in your stoma diagram.

sections.heading: 6.1.2 The Ground Tissue System
sections.body:
NCERT's definition is short and should be quoted as it is: all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles constitute the ground tissue. It consists of simple tissues such as parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. That single sentence is worth 2 marks whenever the examiner asks 'What is ground tissue?'

Where do you find it? Parenchymatous cells are usually present in the cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays in the primary stems and roots. So when you label a T.S., every one of those layers belongs to the ground system, and most of them are parenchyma. The exceptions worth remembering are the hypodermis of the dicot stem (collenchyma) and the hypodermis of the monocot stem (sclerenchyma), which are also ground tissue but not parenchyma, and the semi-lunar patches of sclerenchymatous pericycle above the phloem in a dicot stem.

In leaves the ground tissue consists of thin-walled, chloroplast-containing cells called mesophyll. In a dicot leaf the mesophyll is differentiated into palisade parenchyma and spongy parenchyma; in a monocot leaf it is not differentiated. That difference belongs to section 6.2.5 and 6.2.6, but you should already see that the mesophyll is simply the ground tissue of the leaf.

Function follows cell type. Parenchyma stores food and water, fills space and, when it has chloroplasts, photosynthesises. Collenchyma gives flexible mechanical support to growing organs. Sclerenchyma gives rigid strength. The ground system therefore does the storing, the supporting and (in the leaf) the photosynthesis, while the epidermal system protects and the vascular system conducts.

formulas.expr: Ground tissue = all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles = parenchyma + collenchyma + sclerenchyma
where: cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays (mostly parenchyma)

sections.tip: If asked for the ground tissue of a leaf, the one-word answer is mesophyll. Do not write cortex; leaves have no cortex.

sections.heading: 6.1.3 The Vascular Tissue System
sections.body:
The vascular system consists of the complex tissues, the phloem and the xylem. The xylem and phloem together constitute vascular bundles. Everything the examiner asks in this section is about how the two tissues are placed relative to each other and whether cambium sits between them.

Open versus closed. In dicotyledonous stems, cambium is present between the phloem and the xylem. Such vascular bundles, because of the presence of cambium, possess the ability to form secondary xylem and phloem tissues, and hence are called open vascular bundles. In the monocotyledons the vascular bundles have no cambium present in them. Since they do not form secondary tissues they are referred to as closed. The word open therefore means 'open to further growth', not physically open.

Radial versus conjoint. When xylem and phloem within a vascular bundle are arranged in an alternate manner along different radii, the arrangement is called radial, such as in roots. In the conjoint type of vascular bundles, the xylem and phloem are jointly situated along the same radius of the vascular bundle. Such vascular bundles are common in stems and leaves. The conjoint vascular bundles usually have the phloem located only on the outer side of the xylem.

Put the two classifications together and you get the three drawings in NCERT Figure 6.4, which are asked as 'identify A, B and C': (A) radial, as in a root, with separate xylem and phloem strands on alternate radii; (B) conjoint closed, as in a monocot stem, with phloem outside xylem and no cambium; (C) conjoint open, as in a dicot stem, with a strip of cambium between phloem and xylem. Learn the pairing organ → bundle type: root → radial; dicot stem → conjoint, open, endarch; monocot stem → conjoint, closed, endarch, with a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath.

formulas.expr: Open bundle: cambium present between xylem and phloem (dicot stem) → can form secondary xylem and phloem. Closed bundle: no cambium (monocots)
Radial: xylem and phloem on alternate radii (roots). Conjoint: xylem and phloem on the same radius, phloem outside xylem (stems, leaves)

sections.tip: Radial is about position (different radii), open is about cambium. A root bundle is radial and closed in the primary state; a dicot stem bundle is conjoint and open. Do not mix the two axes.

sections.heading: 6.2 Anatomy of Dicotyledonous and Monocotyledonous Plants: how to read a section
sections.body:
For a clear understanding of tissue organisation, NCERT looks at the transverse sections of the mature zones of the root and stem and a vertical section of the leaf, in a dicot and a monocot each. That gives six sections. The trick to learning them is to fix the order of layers from outside to inside and then note only what changes between monocot and dicot.

For a root the sequence is epiblema (with unicellular root hairs) → cortex → endodermis (casparian strips) → pericycle → vascular bundles (radial, exarch) with conjunctive tissue → pith. Dicot root: two to four xylem bundles, pith small; monocot root: more than six (polyarch), pith large.

For a stem the sequence is epidermis (cuticle, trichomes, few stomata) → hypodermis → cortex → endodermis → pericycle → vascular bundles (conjoint, endarch) → pith. Dicot stem: collenchymatous hypodermis, endodermis as starch sheath, sclerenchymatous pericycle patches, bundles in a ring, open, medullary rays between them, large pith; monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, no distinct cortex, endodermis or pith, bundles scattered, closed, each in a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, phloem parenchyma absent, water-containing cavities present.

For a leaf the sequence is upper (adaxial) epidermis → mesophyll → lower (abaxial) epidermis, with vascular bundles in the veins wrapped by a bundle sheath. Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf: palisade above, spongy below, more stomata on the lower surface, reticulate venation so bundles of varying size; isobilateral (monocot) leaf: undifferentiated mesophyll, stomata on both surfaces, bulliform cells, parallel venation so bundles of nearly similar size.

The exam almost always asks for a diagram plus the differences in a table. Practise drawing each section in under four minutes with eight to ten labels, and practise writing the differences as three-column tables (feature, dicot, monocot). The next six sections give you the NCERT description of each, in the words the marking scheme uses.

formulas.expr: Root: epiblema → cortex → endodermis → pericycle → radial, exarch bundles → pith
Stem: epidermis → hypodermis → cortex → endodermis → pericycle → conjoint, endarch bundles → pith

sections.tip: The most common 1-mark identification: 'radial, exarch, polyarch' = monocot root; 'conjoint, closed, scattered' = monocot stem; 'conjoint, open, in a ring' = dicot stem; 'radial, exarch, 2 to 4 bundles' = dicot root.

sections.heading: 6.2.1 Dicotyledonous Root
sections.body:
Look at NCERT Figure 6.5(a), the T.S. of a sunflower root, and read the layers from outside in.

The outermost layer is the epiblema. Many of the cells of the epiblema protrude in the form of unicellular root hairs. There is no cuticle. The cortex consists of several layers of thin-walled parenchyma cells with intercellular spaces. The innermost layer of the cortex is called the endodermis. It comprises a single layer of barrel-shaped cells without any intercellular spaces. The tangential as well as the radial walls of the endodermal cells have a deposition of water-impermeable, waxy material, suberin, in the form of casparian strips. These strips force water and minerals moving inward to pass through the endodermal cell membrane rather than through the wall, so the endodermis controls what enters the stele.

Next to the endodermis lies the pericycle, a few layers of thick-walled parenchymatous cells. The initiation of lateral roots and of the vascular cambium during secondary growth takes place in these cells. That is the answer to the classic question 'from which layer do lateral roots arise?' (pericycle) and its pair 'from which layer do root hairs arise?' (epiblema, the epidermis).

The pith is small or inconspicuous. The parenchymatous cells which lie between the xylem and the phloem are called conjunctive tissue. There are usually two to four xylem and phloem patches, arranged radially, with the protoxylem pointing outward (exarch). Later, a cambium ring develops between the xylem and the phloem. All tissues on the inner side of the endodermis, such as pericycle, vascular bundles and pith, together constitute the stele.

In the exam, describe the dicot root as: epiblema with unicellular root hairs, parenchymatous cortex, endodermis with casparian strips, pericycle, radial exarch bundles two to four in number, conjunctive tissue, small pith. Each phrase is a marking point.

formulas.expr: Endodermis of root: single layer of barrel-shaped cells, no intercellular spaces, casparian strips of suberin on tangential and radial walls
Stele = pericycle + vascular bundles + pith (everything inside the endodermis)
where: parenchyma between xylem and phloem in the root

sections.tip: Casparian strips are on the tangential AND radial walls. Students write 'radial walls' only and lose the mark. Also note the number: 2 to 4 bundles, and NCERT says the root cambium ring develops 'later'.

sections.heading: 6.2.2 Monocotyledonous Root
sections.body:
The anatomy of the monocot root, NCERT Figure 6.5(b) of a maize root, is similar to the dicot root in many respects. It has an epidermis (epiblema) with unicellular root hairs, a parenchymatous cortex, an endodermis with casparian strips, a pericycle, radial exarch vascular bundles with conjunctive tissue between them, and a pith. So the outer half of your answer is the same as for the dicot root.

The differences are two, and both come from the centre of the section. First, the monocot root has usually more than six xylem bundles; NCERT calls this polyarch, in contrast to the dicot root with two to four. Second, the pith is large and well developed, whereas in the dicot root it is small or inconspicuous. A third point follows from the first two: monocot roots do not undergo any secondary growth, because the pericycle and conjunctive tissue never form a cambium. In the dicot root a cambium ring appears later between xylem and phloem, and the pericycle gives rise to cork cambium, so the dicot root can thicken; the monocot root stays primary for life.

How would you tell a root from a stem in an unlabelled section? Roots have radial bundles with exarch protoxylem and an endodermis with casparian strips; stems have conjoint bundles with endarch protoxylem. And how would you tell a monocot root from a dicot root? Count the xylem groups (more than six versus two to four) and look at the pith (large versus small). Those two questions between them account for most of the 2-mark and 3-mark items on roots.

formulas.expr: Monocot root vs dicot root: xylem bundles polyarch (>6) vs 2–4; pith large vs small; no secondary growth vs cambium ring develops later
where: epiblema with unicellular root hairs, parenchymatous cortex, endodermis with casparian strips, pericycle, radial exarch bundles, conjunctive tissue

sections.tip: For 'polyarch', write 'usually more than six xylem bundles'. The dicot root is 'diarch to tetrarch', though NCERT simply says two to four; use the NCERT phrasing.

sections.heading: 6.2.3 Dicotyledonous Stem
sections.body:
NCERT Figure 6.6(a) shows the T.S. of a sunflower stem. The epidermis is the outermost protective layer of the stem. It is covered with a thin layer of cuticle and may bear trichomes and a few stomata.

The cells arranged in multiple layers between the epidermis and the pericycle constitute the cortex. It has three sub-zones. The outer hypodermis consists of a few layers of collenchymatous cells just below the epidermis, which provide mechanical strength to the young stem. Below it the cortical layers consist of rounded, thin-walled parenchymatous cells with conspicuous intercellular spaces. The innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis. Its cells are rich in starch grains, so the layer is also called the starch sheath. This is the stem's version of the endodermis; there are no casparian strips here in the NCERT description.

The pericycle is present on the inner side of the endodermis and above the phloem bundles in the form of semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma. In between the vascular bundles there are a few layers of radially placed parenchymatous cells which constitute the medullary rays.

A large number of vascular bundles are arranged in a ring; the ring arrangement of vascular bundles is a characteristic of the dicot stem. Each vascular bundle is conjoint, open, and with endarch protoxylem. Phloem lies outside, xylem inside, and a strip of cambium lies between them. A large number of rounded parenchymatous cells with large intercellular spaces occupy the central portion of the stem and constitute the pith.

In the exam: epidermis with cuticle and trichomes; collenchymatous hypodermis; parenchymatous general cortex; endodermis as starch sheath; sclerenchymatous pericycle in semi-lunar patches; conjoint, open, endarch bundles in a ring; medullary rays; large pith. Ten labels, ten marking points.

formulas.expr: Dicot stem cortex = hypodermis (collenchyma) + general cortex (parenchyma) + endodermis (starch sheath)
where: semi-lunar sclerenchyma patches above the phloem

formulas.expr: Dicot stem vascular bundle: conjoint, open, endarch, arranged in a ring

sections.tip: The hypodermis is collenchyma in a dicot stem and sclerenchyma in a monocot stem. This swap is a standard MCQ. Likewise the endodermis of a stem is a starch sheath; casparian strips belong to the root endodermis.

sections.heading: 6.2.4 Monocotyledonous Stem
sections.body:
NCERT Figure 6.6(b), the T.S. of a maize stem, is the one section most students can recognise on sight because of its scattered bundles. The monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis beneath the epidermis, a large number of scattered vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, and a large, conspicuous parenchymatous ground tissue. Because the ground tissue is continuous there is no clear distinction into cortex, endodermis, pericycle and pith; the scattered bundles simply sit in it.

The vascular bundles are conjoint and closed: phloem lies outside xylem on the same radius, and there is no cambium, so the monocot stem never thickens by secondary growth. The peripheral vascular bundles are generally smaller than the centrally located ones. Protoxylem is endarch, as in all stems, and the xylem in each bundle is typically seen as a Y or V shape, with the two large metaxylem vessels forming the arms and the protoxylem at the base.

Two features are unique to the monocot stem and are asked as identifiers: phloem parenchyma is absent, and water-containing cavities are present within the vascular bundles. The water-containing cavity (protoxylem lacuna) forms below the protoxylem when its elements are stretched and torn during elongation of the stem.

The old NCERT exercise remains the model 3-mark question: a T.S. shows conjoint, scattered bundles with sclerenchymatous bundle sheaths and no phloem parenchyma; identify it. Answer: a monocotyledonous stem, because scattered bundles with a bundle sheath and absence of phloem parenchyma are characteristic only of the monocot stem. And if you are handed a fresh section from the school garden, the reasons to call it monocot are: scattered bundles in ground tissue, a bundle sheath around each, closed bundles with no cambium, sclerenchymatous hypodermis, and no differentiation into cortex and pith; to call it dicot: bundles in a ring, open with cambium, collenchymatous hypodermis, distinct cortex, endodermis, pericycle, medullary rays and pith.

formulas.expr: Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis; scattered conjoint closed bundles each in a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; parenchymatous ground tissue; phloem parenchyma absent; water-containing cavities present

sections.tip: Two examiner favourites: 'phloem parenchyma is absent' and 'water-containing cavities are present'. They appear only in the monocot stem description; quote both.

sections.heading: 6.2.5 Dorsiventral (Dicotyledonous) Leaf
sections.body:
A vertical section through the lamina of a dicot leaf (NCERT Figure 6.7(a)) shows three main parts: the epidermis, the mesophyll and the vascular system.

The epidermis covers both the upper surface (adaxial epidermis) and the lower surface (abaxial epidermis) of the leaf, and has a conspicuous cuticle. The abaxial epidermis generally bears more stomata than the adaxial epidermis; the adaxial epidermis may even lack stomata entirely. This unequal distribution is what makes the leaf dorsiventral, with a distinct upper and lower face.

The tissue between the upper and lower epidermis is the mesophyll. Its cells possess chloroplasts and perform photosynthesis, and it is made up of parenchyma. It has two types of cells: the palisade parenchyma and the spongy parenchyma. The adaxially placed palisade parenchyma is made of elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other, packed so that the maximum number of chloroplasts face the light. The spongy parenchyma lies below the palisade cells and extends to the lower epidermis; its cells are oval or round and loosely arranged, with numerous large spaces and air cavities between them, which are continuous with the stomata and allow gas exchange.

The vascular system includes vascular bundles which can be seen in the veins and the midrib. The size of the bundles depends on the size of the veins. The veins vary in thickness in the reticulate venation of dicot leaves, so in a section you see bundles of very different sizes. Each vascular bundle is surrounded by a layer of thick-walled bundle sheath cells. Xylem faces the upper epidermis and phloem the lower, and the bundles are conjoint and closed in the leaf.

For the 5-mark question draw the V.S. with the midrib on one side, label upper epidermis with cuticle, palisade parenchyma, spongy parenchyma with air spaces, lower epidermis with stomata and guard cells, a vascular bundle with xylem above and phloem below inside a bundle sheath, and write the description above in that order.

formulas.expr: Dorsiventral leaf: adaxial epidermis (few or no stomata) → palisade parenchyma (elongated, vertical, parallel) → spongy parenchyma (oval/round, loose, air cavities) → abaxial epidermis (more stomata)
where: in veins and midrib, size varies with vein size (reticulate venation), surrounded by bundle sheath

sections.tip: Palisade cells are 'elongated, arranged vertically and parallel to each other'; spongy cells are 'oval or round, loosely arranged with large air cavities'. These exact adjectives are the marking points.

sections.heading: 6.2.6 Isobilateral (Monocotyledonous) Leaf
sections.body:
The anatomy of the isobilateral leaf (NCERT Figure 6.7(b), a grass leaf) is similar to that of the dorsiventral leaf in many ways: epidermis on both faces with a cuticle, mesophyll between them, vascular bundles in the veins with a bundle sheath. NCERT then lists the differences, and these are the whole examinable content of this section.

First, stomata are present on both surfaces of the epidermis, and in roughly equal numbers, because a grass leaf stands upright and both faces receive similar light. Second, the mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma; all the mesophyll cells look alike. Those two features make the two faces of the leaf equal, hence 'isobilateral'.

Third, in grasses certain adaxial epidermal cells along the veins modify themselves into large, empty, colourless cells called bulliform cells. When the bulliform cells in the leaves have absorbed water and are turgid, the leaf surface is exposed. When they are flaccid due to water stress, they make the leaves curl inwards to minimise water loss. Bulliform cells are a favourite for the 2-mark 'what and why' question and for the case-based passage about a rolled grass leaf on a hot afternoon.

Fourth, the parallel venation in monocot leaves is reflected in the near similar sizes of vascular bundles (except in the main veins) as seen in vertical sections of the leaves. In a dicot leaf, with reticulate venation, bundle size varies widely; in a grass leaf the bundles are evenly spaced and much the same size.

The standard table asked for 3 marks: stomata on lower surface mainly versus both surfaces; mesophyll differentiated versus undifferentiated; bulliform cells absent versus present; reticulate venation with unequal bundles versus parallel venation with similar bundles; dorsiventral (two faces different) versus isobilateral (two faces alike).

formulas.expr: Isobilateral leaf: stomata on both surfaces; mesophyll undifferentiated; bulliform cells in adaxial epidermis along veins; parallel venation → bundles of near similar size
where: large, empty, colourless; turgid → leaf flat and exposed; flaccid → leaf curls inward to reduce water loss

key_terms.definition: The study of the internal structure of plants, seen by cutting thin sections and observing them under a microscope.
A group of cells having a common origin and usually performing a common function.
A grouping of tissues on the basis of their structure and location in the plant body; the three systems are epidermal, ground (fundamental) and vascular (conducting).
The outermost, usually single-layered covering of the primary plant body, made of parenchymatous cells with a large vacuole and often coated with a waxy cuticle.
A waxy, thick layer on the outside of the epidermis that prevents loss of water; absent in roots.
The stomatal aperture, the two guard cells and the surrounding subsidiary cells taken together.

Two bean-shaped (dumb-bell shaped in grasses) chloroplast-containing cells that enclose the stomatal pore; their outer walls are thin and inner walls (towards the pore) are thick, allowing them to open and close the stoma.
A few epidermal cells in the vicinity of the guard cells that become specialised in their shape and size.
Epidermal hairs on the stem; usually multicellular, branched or unbranched, soft or stiff, sometimes secretory; they help prevent water loss by transpiration.
Unicellular elongations of the epidermal (epiblema) cells of the root that absorb water and minerals from the soil.
All tissues except the epidermis and vascular bundles; made of simple tissues (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) and forming cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays and, in leaves, mesophyll.
The ground tissue of a leaf: thin-walled, chloroplast-containing parenchyma between the upper and lower epidermis, differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma in a dicot leaf.
A strand of xylem and phloem together (with cambium in open bundles) that forms the conducting tissue system.
A bundle with cambium between the phloem and xylem, so it can form secondary xylem and phloem; found in dicot stems.
A bundle without cambium, which cannot form secondary tissues; found in monocots.
Arrangement in which xylem and phloem lie in an alternate manner along different radii, as in roots.
Arrangement in which xylem and phloem are jointly situated along the same radius, usually with phloem on the outer side of the xylem; common in stems and leaves.
Endarch: protoxylem towards the centre and metaxylem towards the periphery, as in stems. Exarch: protoxylem towards the periphery and metaxylem towards the centre, as in roots.
The outermost layer of the root (root epidermis), many of whose cells protrude as unicellular root hairs.

The innermost layer of the cortex. In roots it is a single layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces bearing casparian strips; in dicot stems its cells are rich in starch grains and it is called the starch sheath.
Deposits of water-impermeable, waxy suberin on the tangential and radial walls of root endodermal cells.

A few layers of thick-walled parenchymatous cells next to the endodermis in the root; lateral roots and the vascular cambium of secondary growth are initiated here. In the dicot stem it appears as semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma above the phloem.
The parenchymatous cells lying between the xylem and the phloem in a root.
All the tissues on the inner side of the endodermis: pericycle, vascular bundles and pith.
Having many (usually more than six) xylem bundles, as in the monocot root.
The layer just below the epidermis of a stem; collenchymatous in dicot stems (mechanical strength to the young stem) and sclerenchymatous in monocot stems.
A few layers of radially placed parenchymatous cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem.
A layer of thick-walled cells surrounding a vascular bundle; sclerenchymatous around each scattered bundle in a monocot stem, and around the bundles in leaf veins.
The adaxially placed mesophyll of a dicot leaf, made of elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other.
The mesophyll below the palisade layer extending to the lower epidermis; oval or round, loosely arranged cells with numerous large spaces and air cavities between them.

Large, empty, colourless cells formed by modification of certain adaxial epidermal cells along the veins of grass leaves; turgid cells keep the leaf exposed, flaccid cells make it curl inwards to minimise water loss.

A dorsiventral (dicot) leaf has distinct upper and lower faces, with palisade above, spongy below and more stomata on the lower surface; an isobilateral (monocot) leaf has both faces alike, with undifferentiated mesophyll and stomata on both surfaces.

formula_sheet.name: Three tissue systems
formula_sheet.expr: Epidermal (epidermis, stomata, trichomes, root hairs, cuticle); Ground (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma: cortex, endodermis, pericycle, pith, medullary rays, mesophyll); Vascular (xylem + phloem in bundles)
formula_sheet.note: Classified on the basis of structure and location. Standard 3-mark table.

formula_sheet.name: Stomatal apparatus
formula_sheet.expr: Aperture + 2 guard cells + subsidiary cells; guard cells bean-shaped (grasses: dumb-bell), outer wall thin, inner wall thick, contain chloroplasts
formula_sheet.note: Regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Draw both dicot and grass types.

formula_sheet.name: Root hair vs trichome
formula_sheet.expr: Root hair: unicellular, from epiblema, absorbs water and minerals. Trichome: multicellular, on stem, reduces transpiration, may be secretory

formula_sheet.name: Vascular bundle types
formula_sheet.expr: Radial (root: xylem and phloem on alternate radii); Conjoint (stem, leaf: same radius, phloem outside xylem); Open (cambium present, dicot stem); Closed (no cambium, monocots)
formula_sheet.note: NCERT Figure 6.4: identify A radial, B conjoint closed, C conjoint open.

formula_sheet.name: Protoxylem position
formula_sheet.expr: Exarch in roots (protoxylem outside), endarch in stems (protoxylem inside)
formula_sheet.note: Best single clue to tell a root from a stem in an unlabelled section.

formula_sheet.name: Dicot root
formula_sheet.expr: Epiblema with unicellular root hairs → parenchymatous cortex → endodermis (barrel-shaped, no intercellular spaces, casparian strips of suberin on tangential and radial walls) → pericycle (lateral roots, vascular cambium) → 2–4 radial exarch bundles + conjunctive tissue → small pith
formula_sheet.note: Stele = pericycle + vascular bundles + pith. Cambium ring develops later. Example: sunflower.

formula_sheet.name: Monocot root
formula_sheet.expr: Same layers as dicot root but polyarch (usually more than six xylem bundles), large well-developed pith, no secondary growth

formula_sheet.name: Dicot stem
formula_sheet.expr: Epidermis (cuticle, trichomes, few stomata) → collenchymatous hypodermis → parenchymatous cortex → endodermis = starch sheath → sclerenchymatous pericycle in semi-lunar patches → conjoint, open, endarch bundles in a RING with medullary rays between → large parenchymatous pith
formula_sheet.note: Ring arrangement is the characteristic of the dicot stem. Example: sunflower.

formula_sheet.name: Monocot stem
formula_sheet.expr: Epidermis → sclerenchymatous hypodermis → parenchymatous ground tissue with many SCATTERED conjoint, closed bundles each in a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; peripheral bundles smaller; phloem parenchyma absent; water-containing cavities present

formula_sheet.name: Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf
formula_sheet.expr: Adaxial epidermis with cuticle (few/no stomata) → palisade parenchyma (elongated, vertical, parallel) → spongy parenchyma (oval/round, loose, air cavities) → abaxial epidermis (more stomata); bundles in veins and midrib of varying size (reticulate venation), each in a bundle sheath
formula_sheet.note: Xylem towards upper epidermis, phloem towards lower.

formula_sheet.name: Isobilateral (monocot) leaf
formula_sheet.expr: Stomata on both surfaces; mesophyll not differentiated; bulliform cells in adaxial epidermis along veins; parallel venation → bundles of near similar size (except main veins)
formula_sheet.note: Bulliform cells turgid: leaf exposed; flaccid: leaf curls inward to reduce water loss.

formula_sheet.name: Origins to remember
formula_sheet.expr: Root hairs from epiblema; lateral roots from pericycle; vascular cambium of root from pericycle and conjunctive tissue; mechanical strength of young dicot stem from collenchymatous hypodermis
formula_sheet.note: Each is a 1-mark question in its own right.

formula_sheet.name: Background tissues (NEET)
formula_sheet.expr: Meristems: apical, intercalary, lateral. Simple tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma. Xylem: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma. Phloem: sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres
formula_sheet.note: Removed from the CBSE rationalised syllabus but needed to read the chapter and still asked in NEET.

diagrams.title: Stomatal apparatus (NCERT Figure 6.1): dicot stoma and grass stoma
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a surface view of the epidermis with a few irregular epidermal cells. In the centre draw two bean-shaped guard cells facing each other with a lens-shaped pore between them; draw the wall towards the pore as a thick double line and the outer wall thin, put two or three small chloroplasts in each guard cell and a nucleus. Draw two or three subsidiary cells around the guard cells, slightly different in shape from the ordinary epidermal cells. Label: epidermal cell, subsidiary cell, guard cell, chloroplast, nucleus, stomatal pore (aperture), thick inner wall, thin outer wall. Beside it draw a grass stoma with two dumb-bell shaped guard cells and label it 'guard cells of grasses, dumb-bell shaped'.

diagrams.title: T.S. of dicot root (NCERT Figure 6.5a, sunflower)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a circle and, from outside in, a single-cell outer layer with two or three hair-like unicellular extensions, a wide band of rounded cells with spaces, a single ring of barrel-shaped cells drawn tightly with small dark patches on their walls, a thin ring of small cells, and in the centre four star-like xylem groups pointing outward alternating with four small phloem patches, with parenchyma between them and a small central region. Label: epiblema, root hair, cortex, endodermis, casparian strip, pericycle, protoxylem (outer point of each xylem arm), metaxylem (inner), phloem, conjunctive tissue, pith. Write beneath: vascular bundles radial, exarch, tetrarch (2 to 4).

diagrams.title: T.S. of monocot root (NCERT Figure 6.5b, maize)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Same outer layers as the dicot root (epiblema with unicellular root hairs, parenchymatous cortex, endodermis with casparian strips, pericycle). In the stele draw eight or more small xylem groups alternating with phloem patches around a large central pith, with metaxylem vessels drawn as big circles inside the ring and protoxylem as small circles pointing outward. Label: epiblema, root hair, cortex, endodermis, casparian strip, pericycle, protoxylem, metaxylem, phloem, conjunctive tissue, pith (large). Write beneath: polyarch, radial, exarch, no secondary growth.

diagrams.title: T.S. of dicot stem (NCERT Figure 6.6a, sunflower)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a circle. From outside in: a single-cell epidermis with a thick outer line for the cuticle and one or two multicellular trichomes; three or four layers of cells thickened at the corners (collenchymatous hypodermis); several layers of rounded cells with spaces (general cortex); a single layer with dots for starch grains (endodermis / starch sheath). Then draw six to eight vascular bundles arranged in a ring, each with a crescent of sclerenchyma outside (pericycle), phloem below it, a thin band of cambium, then xylem with the smallest vessels innermost (endarch protoxylem). Between bundles draw radial rows of cells (medullary rays). Fill the centre with large rounded cells (pith). Label all ten: epidermis, cuticle, trichome, hypodermis, cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle, phloem, cambium, xylem (protoxylem inner, metaxylem outer), medullary ray, pith. Write beneath: conjoint, open, endarch, in a ring.

diagrams.title: T.S. of monocot stem (NCERT Figure 6.6b, maize)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a circle. Outside: single-cell epidermis with cuticle, then two or three layers of thick-walled sclerenchyma (hypodermis). Fill the rest with rounded parenchyma (ground tissue) and scatter many vascular bundles in it, smaller and closer near the periphery, larger and fewer near the centre. Draw one bundle enlarged beside the section: an outer ring of thick-walled cells (bundle sheath), phloem at the top, then two large metaxylem vessels side by side with a smaller protoxylem vessel below them forming a Y or V, and a space beneath the protoxylem (water-containing cavity / protoxylem lacuna). Label: epidermis, hypodermis (sclerenchymatous), ground tissue, vascular bundle, bundle sheath, phloem, metaxylem, protoxylem, water-containing cavity. Write beneath: conjoint, closed, scattered, endarch; no phloem parenchyma.

diagrams.title: V.S. of dorsiventral (dicot) leaf (NCERT Figure 6.7a)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal strip. Top: a single layer of flat cells with a thick outer line (adaxial epidermis with cuticle). Below it one or two rows of tall, closely packed, vertically elongated cells with many chloroplast dots (palisade parenchyma). Below that several rows of rounded, loosely placed cells with large gaps (spongy parenchyma with air spaces). Bottom: a single layer of cells (abaxial epidermis) with two stomata, each drawn as two guard cells with a pore and an air cavity above it (substomatal chamber). Draw one large vascular bundle in the midrib region and one small one in a vein, each with xylem above and phloem below and a ring of bundle sheath cells around it. Label: cuticle, upper (adaxial) epidermis, palisade parenchyma, spongy parenchyma, air space, lower (abaxial) epidermis, stoma, guard cell, substomatal cavity, xylem, phloem, bundle sheath.

diagrams.title: V.S. of isobilateral (monocot) leaf (NCERT Figure 6.7b, grass)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal strip with upper and lower epidermis both bearing stomata. Fill the middle with one kind of rounded mesophyll cell throughout (no palisade layer). Draw three or four vascular bundles of nearly the same size evenly spaced along the strip, each with xylem up, phloem down and a bundle sheath around it. On the upper epidermis, between two bundles, draw a fan-shaped group of three to five large empty cells (bulliform cells). Label: upper (adaxial) epidermis, lower (abaxial) epidermis, stomata on both surfaces, bulliform cells, undifferentiated mesophyll, vascular bundle, bundle sheath, xylem, phloem. Write beneath: parallel venation, bundles of similar size.

diagrams.title: Types of vascular bundles (NCERT Figure 6.4): radial, conjoint closed, conjoint open
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three small diagrams side by side. (A) Radial: a circle of pericycle with four xylem groups pointing to the centre alternating with four phloem groups, so xylem and phloem lie on different radii; label xylem, phloem, pericycle, 'radial (root)'. (B) Conjoint closed: an oval bundle with phloem at the top, xylem below it on the same radius, no cambium, and a ring of bundle sheath; label phloem, xylem, bundle sheath, 'conjoint closed (monocot stem)'. (C) Conjoint open: phloem at the top, a band of narrow rectangular cambium cells, xylem below; label phloem, cambium, xylem, 'conjoint open (dicot stem)'. Mark the protoxylem towards the centre in B and C (endarch).

diagrams.title: Structure of the endodermis and pericycle of a root (enlarged sector)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a wedge of the root from cortex inward: a few rounded cortical cells, then one row of barrel-shaped endodermal cells drawn tightly with no gaps and with a dark band on the radial walls and the tangential walls (casparian strips), then one or two rows of small thick-walled pericycle cells, then a xylem arm with the narrow protoxylem near the pericycle and wide metaxylem inward, phloem to one side, and parenchyma (conjunctive tissue) between. Add an arrow from the pericycle labelled 'origin of lateral root'. Label: cortex, endodermis, casparian strip, pericycle, protoxylem, metaxylem, phloem, conjunctive tissue.

ncert_questions.q: Draw illustrations to bring out the anatomical difference between (a) monocot root and dicot root, (b) monocot stem and dicot stem.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Root. Draw the T.S. of the dicot root and the monocot root side by side (see the diagrams section). Both show epiblema with unicellular root hairs, parenchymatous cortex, endodermis with casparian strips, pericycle, radial and exarch vascular bundles with conjunctive tissue, and pith. Differences to bring out in the drawings and state below them:

  • Number of xylem bundles: dicot root two to four; monocot root usually more than six (polyarch).
  • Pith: small or inconspicuous in the dicot root; large and well developed in the monocot root.
  • Secondary growth: a cambium ring develops later between xylem and phloem in the dicot root; monocot roots do not undergo any secondary growth.

(b) Stem. Draw the T.S. of the dicot stem and the monocot stem side by side. Differences to bring out:

  • Hypodermis: collenchymatous in the dicot stem; sclerenchymatous in the monocot stem.
  • Ground tissue: differentiated into cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle, medullary rays and pith in the dicot stem; undifferentiated parenchymatous ground tissue in the monocot stem.
  • Arrangement of vascular bundles: in a ring in the dicot stem; scattered, with peripheral bundles smaller, in the monocot stem.
  • Type of bundle: conjoint, open (cambium present) in the dicot stem; conjoint, closed (no cambium) in the monocot stem.
  • Bundle sheath: absent in the dicot stem; sclerenchymatous bundle sheath around each bundle in the monocot stem.
  • Phloem parenchyma: present in the dicot stem; absent in the monocot stem, which instead shows water-containing cavities in the bundles.

ncert_questions.q: Cut a transverse section of young stem of a plant from your school garden and observe it under the microscope. How would you ascertain whether it is a monocot stem or a dicot stem? Give reasons.
ncert_questions.a:
I would look at the arrangement and structure of the vascular bundles and the tissues around them.

It is a dicot stem if: the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring; each bundle is conjoint and open, with a strip of cambium between phloem and xylem; the ground tissue is differentiated into a collenchymatous hypodermis, parenchymatous cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), sclerenchymatous pericycle in semi-lunar patches, medullary rays between the bundles and a large central pith.

It is a monocot stem if: the vascular bundles are scattered in the ground tissue, the peripheral ones being smaller than the central ones; each bundle is conjoint and closed (no cambium) and is surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; the hypodermis is sclerenchymatous; the ground tissue is continuous parenchyma without a distinct cortex, endodermis or pith; phloem parenchyma is absent and water-containing cavities are present in the bundles.

Reason: the ring arrangement of open bundles is characteristic of dicot stems, while scattered closed bundles with bundle sheaths are characteristic of monocot stems.

ncert_questions.q: The transverse section of a plant material shows the following anatomical features: (a) the vascular bundles are conjoint, scattered and surrounded by sclerenchymatous bundle sheaths; (b) phloem parenchyma is absent. What will you identify it as?
ncert_questions.a: It is a monocotyledonous stem. Conjoint vascular bundles occur in stems and leaves, not roots. Scattered vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, are found only in the monocot stem (a dicot stem has its bundles in a ring without bundle sheaths). Absence of phloem parenchyma is a further characteristic of the monocot stem. The bundles would also be closed (no cambium) and show water-containing cavities.

ncert_questions.q: What is stomatal apparatus? Explain the structure of stomata with a labelled diagram.
ncert_questions.a:
The stomatal aperture, the guard cells and the surrounding subsidiary cells are together called the stomatal apparatus.

Structure of stomata: Stomata are minute pores present in the epidermis of leaves that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. Each stoma is composed of two bean-shaped cells called guard cells which enclose the stomatal pore. In grasses the guard cells are dumb-bell shaped. The outer walls of the guard cells (away from the pore) are thin and the inner walls (towards the pore) are highly thickened. Guard cells contain chloroplasts and regulate the opening and closing of stomata: when they are turgid the thin outer walls stretch more than the thick inner walls, the cells curve and the pore opens; when they lose turgor the pore closes. A few epidermal cells near the guard cells become specialised in shape and size and are called subsidiary cells.

Draw the labelled diagram of the stomatal apparatus (guard cells, chloroplasts, nucleus, thick inner wall, thin outer wall, stomatal pore, subsidiary cells, epidermal cells).

ncert_questions.q: Name the three basic tissue systems in the flowering plants. Give the tissue names under each system.
ncert_questions.a:
On the basis of their structure and location there are three tissue systems.

  1. Epidermal tissue system: epidermis (epidermal cells) with cuticle, stomata (guard cells and subsidiary cells), and epidermal appendages such as root hairs and trichomes.
  2. Ground or fundamental tissue system: all tissues except the epidermis and vascular bundles; consists of the simple tissues parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma, forming the cortex, hypodermis, endodermis, pericycle, pith and medullary rays of stems and roots and the mesophyll of leaves.
  3. Vascular or conducting tissue system: the complex tissues xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma) and phloem (sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres), together forming vascular bundles, with cambium in open bundles.

ncert_questions.q: How is the study of plant anatomy useful to us?
ncert_questions.a:
The study of plant anatomy is useful because:

  • It helps us understand the internal organisation of the plant body and how structure relates to function, for example how the palisade parenchyma is built for photosynthesis or how casparian strips in the endodermis control the entry of water into the stele.
  • It allows us to distinguish monocots from dicots and roots from stems from a section alone, using the type and arrangement of vascular bundles.
  • It explains adaptations to the environment, such as bulliform cells that roll grass leaves during water stress, or the thick cuticle of leaves in dry habitats.
  • It has practical uses: identifying timber and fibres (jute and hemp fibres are phloem fibres, ropes are made from sclerenchymatous fibres), understanding how crops grow in girth, detecting adulteration in crude drugs and plant products, and studying the anatomy of fossil plants for evolutionary relationships.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the internal structure of a dorsiventral leaf with the help of labelled diagrams.
ncert_questions.a:
A vertical section through the lamina of a dicot leaf shows three parts: epidermis, mesophyll and vascular system.

Epidermis: present on both the upper (adaxial) and lower (abaxial) surfaces, single-layered, with a conspicuous cuticle. The abaxial epidermis generally bears more stomata than the adaxial one; the adaxial epidermis may lack stomata entirely.

Mesophyll: the parenchymatous tissue between the two epidermal layers; its cells possess chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis. It is differentiated into (i) palisade parenchyma, placed adaxially, of elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other, and (ii) spongy parenchyma, below the palisade cells and extending to the lower epidermis, of oval or round, loosely arranged cells with numerous large spaces and air cavities between them.

Vascular system: vascular bundles are seen in the veins and the midrib. Their size depends on the size of the veins, which vary in thickness in the reticulate venation of dicot leaves. Each bundle is conjoint and closed, with xylem towards the upper epidermis and phloem towards the lower, and is surrounded by a layer of thick-walled bundle sheath cells.

Draw the labelled V.S. of the dorsiventral leaf (cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade parenchyma, spongy parenchyma, air spaces, lower epidermis, stoma with guard cells, xylem, phloem, bundle sheath).

ncert_questions.q: Why is the epidermis of the root without a cuticle, while the epidermis of the stem and leaf has one?
ncert_questions.a: The cuticle is a waxy layer that prevents loss of water from the plant surface. The root epidermis (epiblema) is specialised for absorbing water and minerals from the soil through its unicellular root hairs; a water-impermeable cuticle would stop this absorption, so it is absent in roots. The stem and leaf are exposed to air and would lose water by evaporation, so their epidermis is covered by a cuticle.

ncert_questions.q: Distinguish between the guard cells and the other epidermal cells of a leaf. What is the role of the unequal thickening of guard-cell walls?
ncert_questions.a: Guard cells are bean-shaped (dumb-bell shaped in grasses), occur in pairs enclosing a stomatal pore, contain chloroplasts and have unequally thickened walls; ordinary epidermal cells are irregular in shape, have no chloroplasts, no pore between them and uniformly thin walls, with a small amount of cytoplasm and a large vacuole. The outer wall of a guard cell (away from the pore) is thin and the inner wall (towards the pore) is thick. When the guard cells take up water and become turgid, the thin outer wall stretches more than the thick inner wall, so the cells bow outward and the pore opens; when they lose water they straighten and the pore closes. This is how stomata regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange.

ncert_questions.q: What are bulliform cells? Where are they found and what is their function?
ncert_questions.a: Bulliform cells are large, empty, colourless cells formed by the modification of certain adaxial (upper) epidermal cells along the veins of grass (monocot) leaves. When they have absorbed water and are turgid the leaf surface is exposed; when they are flaccid due to water stress they make the leaf curl inwards, reducing the exposed surface and minimising water loss.

ncert_questions.q: A student examined two unlabelled transverse sections. Section P showed radial vascular bundles with exarch protoxylem and an endodermis with casparian strips; section Q showed conjoint, open vascular bundles with endarch protoxylem arranged in a ring. Identify each section and give reasons.
ncert_questions.a:
Section P is a root (and, if the xylem groups are two to four with a small pith, a dicot root; if more than six with a large pith, a monocot root). Reasons: radial vascular bundles, in which xylem and phloem lie on alternate radii, occur only in roots; exarch protoxylem (protoxylem towards the periphery) is a root character; the endodermis with casparian strips of suberin is characteristic of the root.

Section Q is a dicot stem. Reasons: conjoint bundles (xylem and phloem on the same radius) occur in stems; endarch protoxylem (towards the centre) is a stem character; open bundles with cambium arranged in a ring are found only in the dicot stem, since monocot stem bundles are closed and scattered.

ncert_questions.q: Name the layer of the root from which (a) root hairs and (b) lateral roots arise. Why is the pericycle important during secondary growth?
ncert_questions.a: (a) Root hairs arise as unicellular elongations of the cells of the epiblema (root epidermis). (b) Lateral roots are initiated in the pericycle, the layer of thick-walled parenchymatous cells just inside the endodermis. The pericycle is important during secondary growth because the vascular cambium of the root is initiated partly from pericycle cells (the rest arises from conjunctive tissue), and the pericycle also gives rise to the cork cambium.

pyq.q: Casparian strips are found in the
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The endodermal cells of the root have deposits of suberin on their tangential and radial walls in the form of casparian strips.

pyq.q: Lateral roots originate from the
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: NCERT: the initiation of lateral roots and vascular cambium during secondary growth takes place in the pericycle.

pyq.q: The vascular bundles of a monocot stem are
options: conjoint, open and arranged in a ring
radial, open and arranged in a ring
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Monocot stem bundles have phloem and xylem on the same radius (conjoint), lack cambium (closed) and lie scattered in the ground tissue, each with a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath.

pyq.q: In which of the following is the protoxylem endarch?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: In stems the protoxylem lies towards the centre and metaxylem towards the periphery (endarch); in roots the arrangement is exarch.

pyq.q: Bulliform cells are found in the
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: In grasses certain adaxial epidermal cells along the veins become large, empty, colourless bulliform cells which cause the leaf to curl inward during water stress.

pyq.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a dicot root?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The dicot root has a small or inconspicuous pith; a large well-developed pith is a feature of the monocot root.

pyq.q: The endodermis of a dicot stem is called the starch sheath because
options: its cells are rich in starch grains
it stores starch in the pith
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NCERT: the innermost layer of the cortex of the dicot stem is the endodermis, whose cells are rich in starch grains, so the layer is also called the starch sheath.

pyq.q: Phloem parenchyma is absent and water-containing cavities are present in the vascular bundles of a
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Both features are listed by NCERT only for the monocot stem.

pyq.q: Trichomes on the stem differ from root hairs in being
options: multicellular and helping to prevent water loss
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Root hairs are unicellular extensions of the epiblema that absorb water; trichomes are usually multicellular stem hairs that reduce transpiration and may be secretory.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Guard cells can open and close the stomatal pore by changing shape. Reason (R): The outer wall of a guard cell is thin and the inner wall towards the pore is thick.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The unequal thickening makes the thin outer wall stretch more when the cell is turgid, so the guard cells bow apart and open the pore; R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The vascular bundles of a dicot stem are described as open. Reason (R): Cambium is absent between the xylem and phloem of a dicot stem.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Dicot stem bundles are open precisely because cambium is present between phloem and xylem, which lets them form secondary tissues. R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The epidermis of the root lacks a cuticle. Reason (R): The root epidermis is specialised for absorption of water and minerals through root hairs.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: A waterproof cuticle would block absorption, so it is absent in roots; R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Monocot roots and monocot stems do not undergo secondary growth. Reason (R): Their vascular bundles are closed, that is, they have no cambium.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Secondary xylem and phloem are formed by cambium; monocot bundles lack cambium, so no secondary growth occurs. R explains A.

pyq.q: What is a stomatal apparatus? How do the guard cells of grasses differ from those of other plants?
pyq.answer:
The stomatal aperture, the two guard cells and the surrounding subsidiary cells together constitute the stomatal apparatus. (1 mark)

In most plants the guard cells are bean-shaped; in grasses they are dumb-bell shaped. In both, the outer wall is thin and the inner wall towards the pore is thickened, and the cells contain chloroplasts. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Distinguish between radial and conjoint vascular bundles. Give one example of each.
pyq.answer:
Radial: xylem and phloem are arranged in an alternate manner along different radii; found in roots. (1 mark)

Conjoint: xylem and phloem are jointly situated along the same radius, usually with phloem on the outer side of the xylem; found in stems and leaves. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Why is the endodermis of a dicot stem called the starch sheath? What is the nature of the pericycle in a dicot stem?
pyq.answer:
The endodermal cells of the dicot stem are rich in starch grains, so the layer is called the starch sheath. (1 mark)

In the dicot stem the pericycle lies inside the endodermis, above the phloem of each vascular bundle, as semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma. (1 mark)

pyq.q: What are bulliform cells? Explain their role during water stress.
pyq.answer:
Bulliform cells are large, empty, colourless cells formed from certain adaxial epidermal cells along the veins of grass leaves. (1 mark)

When turgid they keep the leaf surface flat and exposed; when they become flaccid under water stress they make the leaf curl inwards, reducing the exposed surface and minimising water loss. (1 mark)

pyq.q: A transverse section shows radial, exarch vascular bundles with more than six xylem groups and a large pith. Identify the organ and give two reasons.
pyq.answer:
The organ is a monocot root. (1 mark)

Reasons: radial and exarch bundles are found only in roots; more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles with a large, well-developed pith distinguish the monocot root from the dicot root, which has two to four bundles and a small pith. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Give three differences between the anatomy of a dicot root and a monocot root.
pyq.answer:
• Number of xylem bundles: two to four in the dicot root; usually more than six (polyarch) in the monocot root.
  • Pith: small or inconspicuous in the dicot root; large and well developed in the monocot root.
  • Secondary growth: the dicot root later develops a cambium ring between xylem and phloem and undergoes secondary growth; the monocot root does not undergo any secondary growth.

(1 mark for each difference; features common to both, such as epiblema with root hairs, endodermis with casparian strips, pericycle and radial exarch bundles, may be mentioned but earn no extra marks.)

pyq.q: Describe the epidermal tissue system of a flowering plant.
pyq.answer:
The epidermal tissue system forms the outermost covering of the whole plant body and comprises epidermal cells, stomata and epidermal appendages. (½ mark)

Epidermis: usually a single layer of parenchymatous cells with little cytoplasm and a large vacuole, often covered outside by a waxy cuticle that prevents water loss; cuticle is absent in roots. (1 mark)

Stomata: pores in the leaf epidermis bounded by two bean-shaped (dumb-bell shaped in grasses) guard cells with thin outer and thick inner walls and chloroplasts; with the subsidiary cells around them they form the stomatal apparatus and regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange. (1 mark)

Appendages: root hairs are unicellular elongations of epiblema cells that absorb water and minerals; trichomes are usually multicellular hairs on the stem, branched or unbranched, soft or stiff, sometimes secretory, that help prevent water loss. (½ mark)

pyq.q: Differentiate between a dorsiventral leaf and an isobilateral leaf under three headings.
pyq.answer:
• Stomata: dorsiventral leaf has more stomata on the abaxial (lower) epidermis, the adaxial may have none; isobilateral leaf has stomata on both surfaces.
  • Mesophyll: differentiated into adaxial palisade parenchyma and spongy parenchyma in the dorsiventral leaf; not differentiated in the isobilateral leaf.
  • Bulliform cells and vascular bundles: absent in the dorsiventral leaf, whose bundles vary in size because of reticulate venation; present in the adaxial epidermis of the isobilateral (grass) leaf, whose bundles are of nearly similar size because of parallel venation.

(1 mark per difference)

pyq.q: Describe the structure of a vascular bundle of a monocot stem.
pyq.answer:
The vascular bundles of a monocot stem are scattered in the parenchymatous ground tissue, the peripheral bundles being smaller than the central ones. (½ mark)

Each bundle is conjoint (phloem on the outer side of the xylem on the same radius) and closed (no cambium between phloem and xylem, so no secondary growth). (1 mark)

Each bundle is surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath. The xylem is endarch, with two large metaxylem vessels and smaller protoxylem vessels arranged in a Y or V shape. (1 mark)

Phloem parenchyma is absent, and a water-containing cavity is present within the bundle below the protoxylem. (½ mark)

pyq.q: Explain the structure and role of the endodermis and pericycle of a dicot root.
pyq.answer:
Endodermis: the innermost layer of the cortex, a single layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces. Its tangential and radial walls carry casparian strips, deposits of water-impermeable, waxy suberin. Because of the strips, water and minerals must cross the endodermal cell membrane to enter the stele, so the endodermis regulates entry into the vascular tissue. (1½ marks)

Pericycle: a few layers of thick-walled parenchymatous cells lying just inside the endodermis. Lateral roots are initiated in the pericycle, and the vascular cambium of secondary growth is initiated partly from it (the pericycle also gives rise to cork cambium). (1½ marks)

pyq.q: Draw a labelled diagram of the transverse section of a dicot stem and describe the tissues seen from outside to inside.
pyq.answer:
Labelled diagram of the T.S. of a dicot stem (sunflower): epidermis with cuticle and trichome, hypodermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, phloem, cambium, xylem, medullary ray, pith. (2 marks)

Epidermis: outermost single protective layer covered with a thin cuticle; may bear trichomes and a few stomata. (½ mark)

Cortex (between epidermis and pericycle), in three zones: hypodermis of a few layers of collenchyma giving mechanical strength to the young stem; cortical layers of rounded thin-walled parenchyma with intercellular spaces; endodermis, the innermost layer, rich in starch grains and hence called the starch sheath. (1 mark)

Pericycle: semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma inside the endodermis above the phloem. Medullary rays: radially placed parenchyma between the bundles. (½ mark)

Vascular bundles: many, arranged in a ring (characteristic of dicot stems); each conjoint, open (cambium between phloem and xylem) with endarch protoxylem. (½ mark)

Pith: large central region of rounded parenchyma with big intercellular spaces. (½ mark)

pyq.q: With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the internal structure of a dicot root.
pyq.answer:
Labelled diagram of the T.S. of a dicot root (sunflower): epiblema, root hair, cortex, endodermis with casparian strips, pericycle, protoxylem, metaxylem, phloem, conjunctive tissue, pith. (2 marks)

Epiblema: outermost layer, many cells extended as unicellular root hairs; no cuticle. (½ mark)

Cortex: several layers of thin-walled parenchyma with intercellular spaces. (½ mark)

Endodermis: innermost cortical layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces, with casparian strips of suberin on tangential and radial walls. (½ mark)

Pericycle: a few layers of thick-walled parenchyma; site of initiation of lateral roots and vascular cambium. (½ mark)

Vascular tissue: usually two to four radial, exarch xylem and phloem patches with parenchymatous conjunctive tissue between them; a cambium ring develops later between xylem and phloem. Pith small or inconspicuous. All tissues inside the endodermis (pericycle, vascular bundles, pith) form the stele. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Compare the anatomy of a monocot stem and a dicot stem with the help of labelled diagrams.
pyq.answer:
Labelled diagrams of the T.S. of a dicot stem (bundles in a ring, with hypodermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, cambium, medullary rays, pith) and a monocot stem (scattered bundles with bundle sheath in ground tissue, sclerenchymatous hypodermis). (2 marks)

Differences (3 marks, ½ each):

  • Hypodermis: collenchymatous in dicot; sclerenchymatous in monocot.
  • Ground tissue: differentiated into cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle, medullary rays and pith in dicot; undifferentiated parenchyma in monocot.
  • Arrangement of bundles: in a ring in dicot; scattered, peripheral ones smaller, in monocot.
  • Type of bundle: conjoint, open (cambium present, secondary growth possible) in dicot; conjoint, closed (no cambium, no secondary growth) in monocot.
  • Bundle sheath: absent in dicot; sclerenchymatous sheath around each bundle in monocot.
  • Phloem parenchyma: present in dicot; absent in monocot, which has water-containing cavities in its bundles.

pyq.q: Describe the three tissue systems of a flowering plant. Under each, name the tissues and state where they are located in the root, stem and leaf.
pyq.answer:
On the basis of structure and location there are three tissue systems. (½ mark)

1. Epidermal tissue system (1½ marks): the outermost covering of the whole plant body. It consists of the epidermis (single-layered parenchymatous cells with a large vacuole; covered by a cuticle except in roots), stomata (guard cells and subsidiary cells, in the leaf epidermis, regulating transpiration and gaseous exchange) and epidermal appendages (unicellular root hairs on the epiblema of the root; multicellular trichomes on the stem).

2. Ground or fundamental tissue system (1½ marks): all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles, made of the simple tissues parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. In the root and stem it forms the cortex, hypodermis (collenchyma in dicot stem, sclerenchyma in monocot stem), endodermis (casparian strips in the root, starch sheath in the dicot stem), pericycle, medullary rays and pith. In the leaf it forms the mesophyll, thin-walled chloroplast-containing cells differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma in dicots.

3. Vascular or conducting tissue system (1½ marks): the complex tissues xylem and phloem, together forming vascular bundles. Bundles are radial and exarch in roots; conjoint, open and endarch, in a ring in dicot stems; conjoint, closed, scattered with bundle sheaths in monocot stems; conjoint and closed in the veins of leaves within a bundle sheath. Open bundles have cambium and can form secondary xylem and phloem; closed bundles lack cambium.

pyq.q:
A student cut a thin transverse section of a young plant organ and observed it under the microscope. The outermost layer was single and covered by a cuticle with a few multicellular hairs. Below it were a few layers of cells thickened at the corners, then several layers of rounded thin-walled cells, and then a single layer of cells full of starch grains. Inside this, vascular bundles were arranged in a ring; each bundle had a crescent of thick-walled cells outside the phloem, and a band of narrow dividing cells between the phloem and the xylem. The centre was filled with large rounded cells.
(i) Identify the organ and give two reasons.
(ii) Name the layer 'thickened at the corners' and state its function.
(iii) What is the layer 'full of starch grains' called?
(iv) Name the 'band of narrow dividing cells' and state what type of vascular bundle its presence indicates.
pyq.answer:
(i) A dicot stem. Reasons: the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring, and each is conjoint and open with cambium between phloem and xylem; the ground tissue is differentiated into hypodermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle and pith. (1 mark)

(ii) The collenchymatous hypodermis; it provides mechanical strength to the young stem. (1 mark)

(iii) The endodermis, also called the starch sheath because its cells are rich in starch grains. (1 mark)

(iv) The band is the cambium. Its presence makes the bundle an open vascular bundle, able to form secondary xylem and phloem (the crescent of thick-walled cells is the sclerenchymatous pericycle). (1 mark)

pyq.q:
On a hot dry afternoon a student noticed that the leaves of the grass on the school lawn had rolled inwards, while by evening after watering they had flattened out again. A vertical section of one such leaf showed stomata on both surfaces, a mesophyll of uniform cells, several vascular bundles of nearly the same size each enclosed in a sheath, and groups of large empty colourless cells on the upper epidermis between the veins.
(i) Is the leaf dorsiventral or isobilateral? Give two reasons from the observation.
(ii) Name the large empty colourless cells and explain the rolling of the leaves.
(iii) Why are the vascular bundles nearly the same size?
(iv) Name the sheath around each vascular bundle.
pyq.answer:
(i) Isobilateral: stomata are present on both surfaces of the epidermis, and the mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma. (1 mark)

(ii) They are bulliform cells, modified adaxial epidermal cells found along the veins of grass leaves. During water stress they lose water and become flaccid, so the leaf curls inwards, reducing the exposed surface and minimising water loss; after watering they become turgid and the leaf surface is exposed again. (1 mark)

(iii) Monocot leaves have parallel venation, in which the veins are of similar thickness, so the vascular bundles seen in a vertical section are of near similar size (except in the main veins). (1 mark)

(iv) The bundle sheath, a layer of thick-walled cells surrounding each vascular bundle. (1 mark)

phloem lies on both sides of the xylem
it lies at the periphery of the stem

common_mistakes: Writing that the guard cell wall towards the pore is thin. It is the reverse: the inner wall (towards the pore) is thick and the outer wall is thin. Examiners deduct the mark for the mechanism if the walls are swapped.

Confusing the two endodermises. The root endodermis has casparian strips of suberin; the dicot stem endodermis is rich in starch grains and is called the starch sheath. Writing 'casparian strips' in a dicot stem answer loses the mark.
Swapping the hypodermis. Dicot stem hypodermis is collenchyma; monocot stem hypodermis is sclerenchyma. This is the single most common MCQ error in the chapter.

Treating 'open' and 'radial' as opposites. Open versus closed is about cambium; radial versus conjoint is about position. A root bundle is radial and closed; a dicot stem bundle is conjoint and open. Mixing the axes makes an identification answer wrong.
Saying cambium is absent in dicot stems because secondary growth is out of the syllabus. NCERT's rationalised text still says cambium is present in the dicot stem, which is why its bundles are open.
Placing bulliform cells on the lower epidermis or in dicot leaves. They are modified adaxial (upper) epidermal cells along the veins of grass leaves.

Drawing a monocot stem with a distinct cortex, endodermis and pith. The monocot stem has continuous parenchymatous ground tissue with scattered bundles; only the dicot stem has the differentiated zones.
Giving the number of xylem bundles the wrong way round: dicot root two to four, monocot root more than six (polyarch). Also the pith: small in the dicot root, large in the monocot root.
Writing 'root hairs are multicellular'. Root hairs are unicellular elongations of epiblema cells; trichomes on the stem are the multicellular ones.

Unlabelled or partly labelled diagrams. In this chapter the diagram carries 2 marks of a 5-mark question and the marks are for labels in NCERT words; a neat but unlabelled section earns almost nothing.
strategy:
This is a short chapter with a large diagram load, so the preparation plan is simple: learn the three tissue systems in one sitting, then spend most of your time on the six sections.

Day 1 (about 1 hour): read sections 6.1.1 to 6.1.3 and write out the three-system table from memory. Draw the stomatal apparatus twice, once dicot and once grass, with all eight labels. Memorise the four bundle words (radial, conjoint, open, closed) and the two xylem words (exarch, endarch) with the organ each belongs to.

Day 2 (about 2 hours): draw the T.S. of dicot root, monocot root, dicot stem and monocot stem, each with ten labels, timing yourself at four minutes per drawing. Under each drawing write its identifying line: for example 'conjoint, open, endarch, in a ring'. Then write the two three-column difference tables (dicot versus monocot root; dicot versus monocot stem) without looking.

Day 3 (about 1 hour): draw the V.S. of dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves and write the three-column leaf table. Answer NCERT exercises 6.1 to 6.7 in writing; 6.2, 6.3 and 6.7 are the most likely to appear as they are.

What to memorise word for word: the definitions of stomatal apparatus, ground tissue, radial and conjoint bundles, open and closed bundles, casparian strips, bulliform cells and stele; the origins (root hairs from epiblema, lateral roots from pericycle); and the two unique monocot stem lines (phloem parenchyma absent, water-containing cavities present).

In the exam: for any 5-mark question draw first, label in NCERT words, then describe from outside to inside in the same order as the labels. For any 'identify the organ' question, quote the bundle type and protoxylem position as your reasons. Keep the rationalised scope in mind: meristems and secondary growth are not examined by CBSE, but the vocabulary is, so know it.
